notes: gh api on 2026-11-21: by nxt3d (Prem Makeig), opened 2026-11-17T04:44:01Z, merged 2026-11-17T04:53:06Z, commit f9091bc. Text read with git show f9091bc:ERCS/erc-8048.md: ERC-8048 'Onchain Metadata for Token Registries', Draft, created 2025-09-30, authors Prem Makeig and Rafael Abuawad, requires 165, 7930 and 8119. Its Agent Metadata Profile (nicknamed ERC-721T) reserves per-token keys for ERC-721 tokens that represent agents: context; endpoint[<type>] with mcp, a2a, web (aligned with ERC-8004's web service usage), x402 and ens; address[<chain-id>], keyed by the ERC-7930 Chain Identifier; and the optional account[<chain-id>][<index>]. They are read with metadata(uint256,string) and change with the MetadataSet event. New in f9091bc: the profile keys MUST be stored on-chain, on the token contract or a metadata_contract sidecar, and MUST NOT appear in tokenURI or uri JSON; clients MUST read them with metadata(uint256,string) and MUST ignore JSON members with these names; the stated reason is that JSON can change without a MetadataSet event while clients act on these values, for example by sending funds to address[<chain-id>]. The profile predates the change (present at b1f2bd8, 2026-10-10). On 2026-11-11 the same author closed his draft ERC-8156 (PR #1532, Agent Onchain Metadata for ERC-8004 registries) as no longer needed.

title: Setting up your business on ChatGPT
notes: Read with curl GET, HTTP 200 at 2026-11-21T07:07Z UTC; the article was edited several times that morning (page data updatedAt 2026-11-21T05:49:28Z at this read), so it is cited as read 2026-11-21. title: Commerce policies
notes: Read with curl GET, HTTP 200 at 2026-11-21T07:05Z UTC; the page shows 'Updated: September 29, 2026'. The policies set eligibility standards for product listings and merchant participation in OpenAI's shopping experiences, on top of the Usage policies and applicable law. Prohibited products and services include pornography, adult sexual products and gambling services; illegal or regulated drugs, drug paraphernalia, prescription-only medications or medical products, and supplements; counterfeit, stolen and other illicit goods; malware and covert surveillance; alcoholic beverages over 0.5% ABV or kits enabling distillation, and tobacco and nicotine products and their consumption accessories; firearms, ammunition, explosives, illegal or age-restricted weapons and self-defense weapons; recalled or unsafe products; and fake IDs, personal data lists and social media manipulation. They also bar products commonly restricted by payment networks, such as debt relief and credit repair, crypto and NFTs, and travel services with high chargeback risk such as charter flights, timeshares and cruise tickets, as well as high-risk digital entitlements such as in-game currency.

title: Position of the Council at first reading on the Payment Services Regulation (ST 8543/1/26 REV 1)
notes: Dated 2026-11-04 (Brussels) and marked adopted by the Council on 2026-10-29 (procedure 2023/0210(COD)). No AI-agent provision: no hit for agentic, AI agent or autonomous. Recital 170: a pass-through wallet operator that verifies strong customer authentication needs an outsourcing agreement with the payer's PSP, which keeps full liability for the operator's failures to apply it; recitals 16 and 171: technical service providers and payment scheme operators are liable, up to the transaction amount, for failing to support strong customer authentication. Entry into force 20 days after publication, application 21 months later (Article 124). The Legislative Observatory lists the file as awaiting Parliament's second reading, with an indicative plenary date of 2026-12-14 (read 2026-11-14).

notes: Read live on 2026-11-21 (curl GET, HTTP 200 at 07:05Z UTC; openai.com answered plain requests that day). The live post says Wallet was built in partnership with American Express, Chase, Mastercard and Visa. The launch-day text, in the Internet Archive capture of 2026-11-13T16:04:07Z (archiveUrl, read 2026-11-14 while openai.com refused automated reads), named American Express, Mastercard and Visa. Chase appears only in the partner sentence; the quote carousel still has three entries, from American Express (Luke Gebb, who calls Wallet the first American Express Agentic Commerce Experiences integration), Mastercard and Visa. The rest matches the capture: Wallet is initially available through dots for ChatGPT Pro subscribers in the US aged 18 and older with eligible US-issued cards and begins rolling out that day; the user adds a card once, reviews the items, total and selected card before each purchase and approves with a security check such as Face ID or a fingerprint scan, and each approval creates a record of the authorized purchase; after approval the payment network provides a payment token with a card number, security code and expiration date, so neither the business nor the agent sees the actual card details; users keep card rewards and protections for eligible disputes, and businesses keep pricing, fulfillment, returns and customer service; fraud prevention partners include Forter, Riskified, Sardine and Signifyd and PSPs include Adyen, Checkout.com and Stripe (lists marked as not exhaustive); risk systems may still decline legitimate agent purchases; ChatGPT has 1.2B weekly users; delegation within spending limits, categories or time periods is described as a future expectation without a date. Its meta, og and twitter descriptions, like OpenAI's RSS description (src-openai-news-rss-20261114, src-openai-acp-news-rss-20261121), still name agents in ChatGPT Work, Codex and dots; the post body names dots only, and OpenAI's help article says Wallet works only in conversations with a dot (src-openai-wallet-help-purchases).

title: Accept payments (Commerce in ChatGPT, OpenAI developer docs)
notes: Read through the .md twin (HTTP 200 at 2026-11-15T02:47Z UTC). Customers can pay with ChatGPT Wallet on the business's website or use a payment method already saved there, after approving in ChatGPT; the business handles the order, fulfillment, customer support and fraud decisions. Wallet works with existing checkout pages and payment forms, with no Wallet-specific integration. The merchant receives a network token instead of the card number and can use the Payment Account Reference (PAR) to link it to the account; the customer consents only to the specific transaction, so the credential must not be reused or saved for another purchase; subscriptions work if the checkout supports recurring billing, with the customer's consent and the processor's practice for merchant-initiated transactions; Wallet is a separate option beside an existing card-on-file flow. OpenAI says it is rolling out user signals in the Forwarded HTTP header with the parameters asn, for, ip-country, ip-prefix, locale, tz and user-agent, and that the signals may vary during the rollout. title: Help ensure cloud browser access to your site (Commerce in ChatGPT, OpenAI developer docs)
notes: Read through the .md twin (9,847 bytes, HTTP 200 at 2026-11-21T07:07Z UTC); the page has no date. It says a firewall may block or interrupt cloud browser visits made on a user's behalf and, to help those requests go through reliably, tells sites to add ChatGPT's agent profile to the firewall's allowlist while keeping other security controls in place; a site that applies an allowlist exception for signed browser requests should verify their signatures first. Its FAQ says an allowlist rule for verified cloud browser visits does not change how the site handles other traffic and that an exception can apply site-wide. Akamai, Cloudflare, HUMAN and Vercel verify the signatures automatically. Provider identifiers: Akamai lists the traffic as ChatGPT Agent in its AI Fetchers and Agents category; Cloudflare shows dots, OpenAI under Personal Agents or, for WAF custom rules, bot tag chatgpt-agent and detection ID 129220581, found by searching for ChatGPT Operator; HUMAN lists ChatGPT Agent in Sightline Known Bots & Crawlers and under AgenticTrust AI Agents Permissions; Vercel recognizes the ChatGPT Agent entry, identified as chatgpt-operator, and a Vercel-hosted site whose rules do not block the traffic needs no additional configuration. ChatGPT uses Web Bot Auth (RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signatures) to identify certain cloud browser requests, not web crawlers: a signed request carries Signature and Signature-Input headers and a Signature-Agent header set to the quoted string https://chatgpt.com, and keys are published at https://chatgpt.com/.well-known/http-message-signatures-directory. FAQ: site owners cannot yet control which actions users take, but OpenAI requires human review before any consequential action across all users; browser access needs no product feed or plugin; OpenAI says customers are ultimately responsible for the actions they take, so support follows the business's normal process. The page does not say whether the signature covers the Forwarded header. This record's note of the 2026-11-14 read said the cloud browser needs no allowlist, and that was right when read: the page's Internet Archive captures of 2026-11-14T13:37:10Z and 2026-11-15T16:07:26Z (same digest, read 2026-11-21) still say a site does not need to add the cloud browser to an allowlist, so OpenAI changed the page after 2026-11-15T16:07Z and gives no date for the change.

title: Making purchases with ChatGPT Wallet
notes: Read with curl GET, HTTP 200 at 2026-11-21T07:05Z UTC. The page data gives updatedAt 2026-11-19T23:24:49Z (the page shows 'Updated: yesterday'); no first-publication date is shown. Availability: Wallet is rolling out gradually to eligible ChatGPT Pro users in the US; it works in conversations with a dot, the user sets up a dot first, and it is not available in Chat, Work or standalone Codex threads; approving a purchase requires biometric verification, such as Face ID or Touch ID, on a supported device. Cards: eligible US-issued American Express, Chase, Mastercard and Visa cards; the user must be 18 or older, live in the US and have a US billing address for the card; only the primary cardholder can add an eligible Chase card, not an authorized user, and the user approves the connection in the Chase mobile app, scanning a QR code when starting on a computer; the bank may ask to verify the card during setup with a code or an approval in its app; some US-issued debit cards are supported, but Chase debit cards are not; virtual cards cannot be added at launch, which is separate from the virtual card number Wallet uses for an approved purchase. Purchases: after approval the dot uses a virtual card number linked to the selected card, so the number entered at checkout may differ from the physical card, and the FAQ says Wallet generates a payment token for each use; if the user agrees to a recurring or continuous payment plan, the merchant may store the credential and charge it again under those terms; 'Ready to check out' means the approval is complete and does not confirm that the merchant placed the order; Wallet may not complete checkout at every store. Help: the merchant handles order status, cancellations, returns and refunds; the card issuer handles declined, pending, disputed or unrecognized charges and bank verification problems; OpenAI Support handles Wallet errors, suspected account access and purchases that differ from what the user approved.

title: Agent Communication Protocols (agentproto) charter, charter-ietf-agentproto-01
notes: Text read in full from https://www.ietf.org/charter/charter-ietf-agentproto-01.txt (HTTP 200, 8,678 bytes, 2026-11-21). Group API: agentproto, Applications and Real-Time (ART) area, active. Group events: created in BOF state 2026-06-11 with AD Charles Eckel; chairs Leslie Daigle and Orie Steele from 2026-06-15; list renamed from agent2agent to agentproto on 2026-07-24; Proposed 2026-09-09; charter approved and group active 2026-10-08T16:55:05Z. Scope: a common baseline agentic dialog management protocol (dialog identifiers, lifecycle semantics and propagation of dialog context, with bindings over existing IETF protocols such as HTTP, QUIC, WebTransport, WebRTC or MoQ), an informational reference architecture and an informational use cases and requirements document. The protocol is not meant to replace application-layer agent protocols or to be a new transport; MCP and A2A are expected to carry the dialog context in their own way, and changing those protocols is left to their maintainers, outside the group's scope. Milestones: adopt a use cases draft by 2026-12-31, an architecture draft by 2027-02-28 and protocol drafts by 2027-03-31; submit the protocol to the IESG by 2028-03-31.

notes: Read 2026-11-14 (HTTP 200, 2026-11-15T04:48Z UTC); page last updated 2026-08-14. title: ChatGPT Wallet Privacy Notice
notes: Read with curl GET, HTTP 200 at 2026-11-21T07:05Z UTC; the page shows 'Effective: November 12, 2026'. It names OpenAI OpCo, LLC and covers Wallet use in the US. A service provider collects the card number, expiration date, security code, billing address and other verification data in a secure form; OpenAI receives a tokenized payment credential and limited card details (network, issuer, card type, last four digits, expiration date, billing country or postal code, and eligibility and status signals) and does not receive the full card number or security code. OpenAI also keeps purchase records, including the approval or rejection and the authentication result, collects device, security and fraud signals, and receives token, transaction and fraud data from merchants, issuers, card networks and payment providers. It discloses information to payment and security providers, to merchants and their providers, and to card issuers and payment networks, and says it does not sell Wallet information or share it for cross-context behavioral or targeted advertising.

title: ChatGPT Wallet terms
notes: Read with curl GET, HTTP 200 at 2026-11-21T07:05Z UTC; the page shows 'Effective: November 12, 2026'. Section 1: Wallet lets eligible users save an eligible card and direct ChatGPT to use a payment credential linked to it; it does not create a bank account or stored balance, extend credit, transfer funds or change the user's relationship with the card issuer; the user must review and approve each purchase before it is submitted or grant ChatGPT the authority to approve each purchase in advance. Section 2: the user must be 18 or older, live in the US, have a US billing address for the credit card and use a card issued by a US financial institution; a business card is allowed if the organization permits it. Section 3: the issuer or OpenAI's payment service provider may place a temporary verification authorization, which is reversed. Section 5: after approval OpenAI may ask a payment service provider, card network or issuer to create or provide a tokenized, virtual or other payment credential linked to the card; the credential may differ from the printed number, but the purchase is charged to the card account; the issuer decides whether to authorize and the merchant whether to accept. Section 6: the merchant is the seller and merchant of record; OpenAI is not a bank, card issuer, payment network, lender or merchant for Wallet purchases and does not hold purchase funds. Section 7: the cardholder agreement and issuer and network rules, including dispute and unauthorized-transaction rights, still apply; OpenAI does not decide or fund merchant refunds or card chargebacks unless required by law or it separately promises otherwise. Section 9: Wallet may not be used for fraud, money laundering, cash-equivalent transactions, illegal goods or services or sanctions evasion, and OpenAI may set transaction, merchant, category, card, account, device or geographic limits. The terms name no alcohol rule.

title: Sybil Resistance in Reputations for Agentic Marketplaces
notes: Read 2026-11-21 (curl GET, HTTP 200; page dated November 13, 2026; authors Reza Ramji, Preston Vander Vos and Duc Le of Circle Research). Introduces Anduin, which rates x402 service providers from the payment graph (who pays whom), so that to look trusted to an agent an attacker must spend real money at the services that agent already uses. Circle says that on 66 million real x402 payments (66.1 million settlements worth $6.1 million over 157 days, 2026-03-23 to 2026-08-26, on 16 networks: 15 EVM chains and Solana) Anduin recommends providers about as accurately as the best standard method, collaborative filtering, which it does not beat on accuracy, while being about 23 times more expensive to manipulate in the tested attack; it needs no change to x402, HTTP payment headers or ERC standards. Circle also says fewer than 4,000 voluntary on-chain ratings (for example ERC-8004 feedback) were recorded across those payments. The post notes that Circle Research projects are not completed or released software or services. Research paper: arXiv 2611.05586 (src-orbit-circle-anduin-arxiv).

title: Anduin: A sybil-resistant agentic marketplace reputation system
notes: Abstract page read 2026-11-21 (curl GET, HTTP 200). Reza Ramji, Preston Vander Vos, Ziming Zeng and Duc V. Le; primary category cs.AI; only v1 (Tue, 3 Nov 2026 20:17:03 UTC). The abstract models payment flows as a bipartite graph between buyers and providers over a 157-day dataset of 66 million agentic transactions worth $6.1 million on 16 blockchains, proposes three Sybil-resistant ratings, and reports that against simulated adversaries across 813 buyers rating manipulation costs 20 percent of those buyers' total spend, about 23 times harder than collaborative filtering. title: Payment validation (Cloudflare Monetization Gateway docs)
notes: Read 2026-11-14 through the .md twin (HTTP 200, 2026-11-15T04:58Z UTC). The page was last updated 2026-09-30 (dateModified 2026-09-30), so this text predates the 2026-10-11 check of the orbit page. The origin receives the payment authorization as a JWT in a PAYMENT-CONTEXT header and must verify it (Ed25519, pinned JWKS at https://payments.cloudflare.com/certs) before serving paid content. Fixed pricing uses the x402 exact scheme and settles the signed amount. Variable pricing uses upto: the JWT carries the authorized maximum, and after a successful response the origin sets a PAYMENT-SETTLEMENT header with the actual amount. Above the maximum the gateway settles the maximum, at zero nothing is settled, and the gateway removes PAYMENT-SETTLEMENT from the response sent to the buyer.

title: Crossmint Launches Agentic Cards API Using Visa Intelligent Commerce and Basis Theory
Introducing Menta: Open-Source Plugin for Agentic Commerce
notes: Read 2026-11-21 (curl GET, HTTP 200; JSON-LD datePublished and dateModified 2026-11-18). Menta is an open-source agentic commerce plugin built on Crossmint's Agent Commerce Toolkit (launched in October) that lets an AI assistant buy for its user. It is in the ChatGPT, Devin and Grok Bot plugin marketplaces; for Claude, Muse and other assistants the user pastes a setup prompt from menta.crossmint.com. The card stays in a PCI-compliant vault and the assistant never sees the number; the user approves a spending limit and how long it lasts, or approves every purchase. Menta checks out through the store's own API, an agent protocol or a browser built for checkout, names no protocol, accepts cards issued around the world, and pays with the user's own card (the post says no one-time virtual cards) or a card saved in the store account, Shop Pay, Pix or Bizum. Crossmint says that in its test at 3,000 stores Menta completed 91 percent of purchases, 5 to 10 times faster than general-purpose agents using browser checkouts, and warns that it will not get every store right yet. The post states no price.

title: Update ERC-8226: Scope mandates by target with actions and limits (ethereum/ERCs PR #2191)
notes: gh api repos/ethereum/ERCs/pulls/2191 on 2026-11-21: opened 2026-11-20T10:52:29Z by thamerdridi (Thamer Dridi, Brickken), merged 2026-11-20T11:14:10Z by eip-review-bot, merge commit 9912307 (99123078478fb56b1b5a5abcbb6b6207dba70832), 17 files, +1,801 -1,051. Text read with git show 9912307:ERCS/erc-8226.md (750 lines) in research/vendor/ERCs and compared with 9912307^, the text of PR #2060 (commit f4df3d0, 2026-10-09). Status still Draft and description unchanged (a compliance delegation layer for AI agents operating on tokenized regulated assets). New: mandates keyed by (agent, principal, target), the target being the contract the agent calls, instead of (agent, principal, asset); the scope is a list of actions (bytes32 labels, each with calldata constraints: index, check EQUALS, NOT_EQUALS, AT_MOST or AT_LEAST, value; several EQUALS constraints on one index form an allowlist) plus limits per asset and direction (OUTFLOW or INFLOW) with maxTransactionValue, maxCumulativeValue and cumulativeUsed, shared by all the mandate's actions; canExecute and recordExecution take (agent, principal, target, action, data, flows), a flow being (asset, direction, amount); a non-zero flow with no matching limit fails with NO_LIMIT; new reasons CONSTRAINT_FAILED and NO_LIMIT; recordExecution reverts with MandateBlocked(reason); a new grant clears the prior actions and limits, and the signer sets each limit's starting cumulativeUsed; an approved operator may grant, revoke and extend mandates, directly or by signature, but may not set operators; only the principal approves operators, and an enforcer may call setOperator only to remove one; enforcers freeze and cannot revoke; ERC-165 ids IAgentMandate 0x5aa4c7e4 and IComplianceProvider 0xfa2a39b3; RAMS now defines three interfaces, IAgentExecutor OPTIONAL. Already in the 2026-10-09 text: the three enforcement venues (token gate, EIP-7702 account, executor) and IAgentExecutor as an OPTIONAL, non-normative companion interface, and operators could already revoke and extend. Moved or changed: IAgentExecutor into the Specification; the account venue as one stateless EIP-7702 delegate code deployment per chain and registry, or a module such as a Safe module (which needs the recorder role); a standalone executor for EVM chains without EIP-7702 that MUST serve one principal; executors SHOULD measure the principal's balance changes around each call. The text still names ERC-8004 as an example identity layer and does not mention AP2, x402 or any card network.

title: The 402 (Payment Required) HTTP Status Code (draft-nottingham-httpbis-402-00)
publisher: IETF Datatracker (individual draft; M. Nottingham, Cloudflare)
notes: Doc API, HTTP 200, 2026-11-21: rev 00 posted 2026-10-18T07:12:01Z, expires 2027-04-21 (the text's face is dated 30 August 2026); individual submission, intended status Standards Track. Text read in full from https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-nottingham-httpbis-402-00.txt (7,608 bytes). It defines 402 to mean that payment is needed for the request to succeed and that none the server accepts has been made yet; the code says nothing about the form of payment or what it covers. A server that sends 402 SHOULD say how a payment can be made, in header fields or content; any server, including an intermediary, may send it; a 402 response is not heuristically cacheable; clients SHOULD NOT act on payment information that did not arrive over an authenticated connection; clients that pay without direct human involvement need limits on how much, how often and to whom. IANA would only point the existing 402 entry at the document; it adds no registry or header field. Not adopted by the HTTP working group on 2026-11-21.

title: MCP specification 2026-07-28, Base Protocol: Error Codes
notes: Read from docs/specification/2026-07-28/basic/index.mdx at main through gh api, 2026-11-21; the Error Codes section is identical to the one at commit db4bfcf (2026-07-28). MCP splits the JSON-RPC implementation-defined range -32000 to -32099: -32000 to -32019 is legacy, and -32020 to -32099 is reserved for codes the MCP specification defines and records in its schema, and an implementation may not send any code from that sub-range that the specification does not define. Defined codes: -32020 HeaderMismatch, -32021 MissingRequiredClientCapability, -32022 UnsupportedProtocolVersion. Codes from earlier versions stay reserved, and an implementation of 2026-07-28 may not send -32002 (resource not found, 2025-11-25 and earlier) or -32042 (URL elicitation required, 2025-11-25 only). New application codes should be allocated outside -32768 to -32000.

title: OAuth client could send credentials to an authorization server chosen by the MCP server (GHSA-qx49-fqc8-xw99)
notes: gh api GET repos/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk/security-advisories/GHSA-qx49-fqc8-xw99, 2026-11-21: published 2026-09-28T20:06:03Z, updated 2026-10-23; CVE-2026-115563; severity high, CVSS 3.1 score 7.5 (6.5 when scored for the interactive OAuthClientProvider); CWE-345 and CWE-522. Affected pip package mcp >= 1.9.1, < 1.30.0 and >= 2.0.0a1, < 2.2.0; fixed in 1.30.0 and 2.2.0, both released 2026-09-07. The OAuth client support (mcp.client.auth) skipped the issuer check on authorization server metadata on some discovery paths and left stored or pre-provisioned client credentials unbound to their authorization server, so an MCP server that is hostile or compromised could have the client_secret, the authorization code and the PKCE code_verifier, or a signed client assertion with PrivateKeyJWTOAuthProvider, sent to a token endpoint that it picks. After upgrading, ClientCredentialsOAuthProvider and PrivateKeyJWTOAuthProvider still follow the authorization server the MCP server advertises unless given issuer= (a deprecation warning now, required in 3.0). Not affected: MCP servers built with the SDK, stdio clients, clients that attach their own tokens or headers. The GitHub Advisory Database added the reviewed global entry (https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qx49-fqc8-xw99) on 2026-11-19T22:45:40Z and NVD published the CVE on 2026-11-16; the disclosure and the fix are older. An SDK flaw, not a change to the MCP specification.

title: SEP-3415: Events Extension
notes: gh api GET contents, 2026-11-21: Status Final, Extensions Track, created 2026-10-05, author and sponsor Peter Alexander; merged in commit 8a18b4b at 2026-11-19T15:06:34Z. Extension identifier io.modelcontextprotocol/events, owned by the Tasks and Events Working Group, and applicable to protocol revision 2026-07-28 onward; the specification is published in the ext-events repository under specification/beta/events/. A server lists event types with events/list. Three optional delivery modes: poll (events/poll), push (events/stream, a long-lived request that delivers notifications) and webhook (events/subscribe, signed POSTs to an https callback under a TTL that the client refreshes). A cursor that only the server interprets lets a client pick up where it left off, and event payloads count as untrusted data, as tool results do. Under SEP-3392 (extension lifecycle) an Extensions Track SEP moves an extension into Beta. MCP itself had no specification release after 2026-07-28 on 2026-11-21.

title: Agent Auth (AAuth) Working Group Charter
notes: gh api GET contents/charter.md, 2026-11-21; the file's only commit is 27e1b36 (2026-11-10T17:51:26Z); the repository was created 2026-11-05T18:00:03Z with a README only. Scope: agent identity, with a proof-of-possession check on each request and no need for pre-registration or shared secrets; person identity building on OpenID Connect and other OIDF specifications; authorization across trust domains; agent governance (missions, consent and oversight); delegation; discovery and trust; events and lifecycle; conformance and compliance testing; security and privacy. Out of scope: how a person server decides on or authenticates the person, agent runtime and model behavior, payment protocols, and changes to OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect or HTTP Message Signatures (RFC 9421). Proposed specifications with target dates (Implementers Draft, then Final): AAuth Protocol 1.0 Q2 2027 and Q1 2028; AAuth Supervision 1.0 Q3 2027 and Q2 2028; HTTP Signature Keys 1.0 Q1 2027 and Q4 2027; AAuth Events 1.0 Q4 2027 and Q2 2028; AAuth Rich Resource Requests (R3) 1.0 Q4 2027 and Q3 2028; AAuth Budgets 1.0 Q1 2028 and Q3 2028. The audience includes MCP servers. Liaisons include the IETF OAuth, HTTP, WIMSE and webbotauth groups and the Linux Foundation MCP and A2A projects. Proposers Dick Hardt, Wayne Chang (SpruceID), Jared Hanson (Keycard), Karl McGuinness and Christian Posta; proposed editor Dick Hardt. The dates are plans and the scope is not yet approved.

The post quotes Sarah Cecchetti (Semperis), chair of the AI Threat Modeling Group, a subgroup of the AIIM community group, and thanks the threat modeling and taxonomy subgroups. Threats covered: telling which agent is actually acting; whether two domains trust each other's keys and assertions; an agent acting on the wrong resource once it crosses a boundary; permissions that widen in translation between domains; access that lasts beyond its task; and credentials that are captured and replayed. It traces them all to handling agents like human users and favors controls at authorization time over detection afterwards. A threat model, not a specification or a protocol.

publisher: Personal Agent Protocol project (Sierra and Meta with design partners)
notes: Read through the .md variant (HTTP 200, 2026-11-15T02:55Z UTC). Covers discovery (a poppy.json document at /.well-known/poppy.json, HTTPS only), OAuth account access (Direct Sign-In, Device Sign-In; private_key_jwt client assertions from a client metadata document), Sessions (a Poppy-Session header on every request to a Company's APIs and protocol endpoints: a per-request JWT with typ poppy-session+jwt, signed with a delegated key that a key in the Personal Agent's jwks_uri vouches for; the User ID is pairwise per Company) and channels (web browsing, APIs, conversations with a Company Agent). UCP's Business, Platform and Buyer are this protocol's Company, Personal Agent and User. The agent fetches the UCP profile at /.well-known/ucp (no redirects), sends Poppy-Session on UCP requests, and one RFC 9421 signature can serve both protocols when it covers poppy-session and authorization plus the components UCP's signature rules name. Action items for draft-ietf-webbotauth-httpsig-protocol, recorded as room outcomes, not draft text: swap the tag, whose values nobody coordinates, for a dedicated signature parameter or a required set of covered headers; set a minimal baseline of signed components (authority or host, signature-agent, freshness) so servers cannot demand more; define standard response headers, at SHOULD level, that report why verification failed; add text on centralization risks for independent crawlers to the security and privacy considerations, with input from Nick Doty. The presenters' summary of -01 keeps replay detection and nonces deferred to possible extensions. Scope: Signed Agent Metadata and PACE (which composes Web Bot Auth with MOLE) re-confirmed as out of scope for the current charter, as the chairs read it for per-user, per-session and sub-agent tracking; non-cryptographic IP range publishing (SAIL) outside the charter, with the chairs to consult the AD, Mike Bishop. Participants interested in privacy-preserving rate limiting were directed to the MOLE venue. Implementer feedback: the move of Signature-Agent from a string to a dictionary caused parsing failures; query parameters should stay out of the default signature base. The web-bot-auth@ietf.org archive (browse page read 2026-11-21, posts up to 2026-11-18) showed no chair confirmation of the room consensus.

title: Stablecoin Regulations (proposed), Canada Gazette, Part I, Vol. 160, No. 43
notes: Read 2026-11-14 (HTTP 200, 2026-11-15T03:41Z UTC). Prepublished 2026-10-24 under the Stablecoin Act and the Retail Payment Activities Act, with representations invited within 60 days of publication. The Regulatory Impact Analysis Statement says the proposed Regulations would come into force alongside the Stablecoin Act on a day or days fixed by order of the Governor in Council, with the intention of fall 2027. Issuer rules cover Bank of Canada registration, one-to-one reserves, redemption with capped fees, governance, risk, data security and recovery, and no yield. An amendment to the Retail Payment Activities Regulations treats a unit as meeting prescribed criteria if it is a stablecoin issued by an issuer on the Bank of Canada's list (or by a financial institution under substantially similar law), so payment service providers that perform payment functions with such stablecoins would have to register with the Bank of Canada and meet its safeguarding and operational-risk rules, while financial institutions that issue such stablecoins would not themselves be subject to the Retail Payment Activities Act. Proposed, not final. Canada Gazette Part II issues of 2026-10-07, 2026-10-21 and 2026-11-04 carry no commencement order for the Stablecoin Act.

title: Position of the Council at first reading on the Payment Services Directive (PSD3) (ST 8535/1/26 REV 1, 2023/0209(COD))
notes: PDF text read 2026-11-14 (184 pages, dated Brussels, 2026-11-04, headed as adopted by the Council on 2026-10-29). Article 49: Member States transpose and apply the Directive 21 months after entry into force; Article 48 repeals PSD2 (Directive (EU) 2015/2366) and the second E-Money Directive (2009/110/EC) from the same date; Article 43 lets already authorized payment institutions continue until 27 months after entry into force. Article 47 inserts a new MiCA Article 60(4a): a payment institution may provide crypto-asset services in relation to e-money tokens for the purposes of its payment services, where they are equivalent to the payment services it is authorized for, if it notifies its home competent authority at least 40 working days before it starts. No provision addresses AI agents.

title: Position of the Council at first reading on the Payment Services Regulation (ST 8543/1/26 REV 1, 2023/0210(COD))
notes: PDF text read 2026-11-14 (389 pages, dated Brussels, 2026-11-04, headed as adopted by the Council on 2026-10-29). Article 124: entry into force on the twentieth day after publication in the Official Journal; most provisions apply 21 months after entry into force, Articles 51 and 58 after 27 months, and Articles 92 and 118 from entry into force. The recitals deem e-money tokens to be electronic money and say that transfer services for e-money tokens on behalf of clients could qualify as the payment service of executing payment transactions; recital 29 excludes trading and exchange of e-money tokens but not their transfer to pay for goods or services. Recitals relevant to agent payments: 158 (strong customer authentication applies when the initial merchant-initiated mandate is set up, not to each later merchant-initiated transaction), 162 (European Digital Identity Wallets as a means of authentication), 170 (operators of pass-through wallets need outsourcing agreements and the payer's PSP keeps full liability), 16 and 171 (technical service providers and payment schemes are liable for failing to support strong customer authentication, capped at the transaction amount). No provision addresses AI agents: 'artificial intelligence' appears once, in a fraud-monitoring recital, and 'agentic', 'AI agent' and 'autonomous' have no hits.

title: Proposal for a Regulation on promoting fair business-to-consumer commercial practices in the offline and digital single market, and repealing Directive 2005/29/EC (Digital Fairness Act), COM(2026) 1100 final
notes: Commission document page and its PDF read 2026-11-21 (curl GET, HTTP 200; PDF 512,328 bytes, text extracted locally). Cover: Brussels, 11.11.2026, COM(2026) 1100 final, procedure 2026/0356 (COD). The canonical text is on EUR-Lex (CELEX 52026PC1100, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:52026PC1100), which answered HTTP 202 with an empty body to the first read on 2026-11-21; a later read the same day (HTTP 200, 418,361 bytes) showed the same Article 3(21) definition and the same Articles 26, 27 and 40, and Article 26(7) has the consumer's system send the consumer's contact details to the trader. A proposed regulation that would repeal the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive 2005/29/EC; companion proposals amend Directives 2011/83/EU and 2002/58/EC for simplification (COM(2026) 1110) and revise the CPC Regulation (COM(2026) 1120). Article 3(21) defines an automated system as software capable of carrying out actions and taking decisions producing legal effects for its user, including concluding contracts, without the need for human intervention. Article 26 (automated systems for contracting on behalf of a consumer with a trader) binds traders that make such systems available to consumers: tools to express choices and set and adjust the parameters at any time (26(1)); at first use the consumer must expressly choose to confirm all contracts, to confirm only a type of contracts based on criteria the consumer sets, including a maximum price and a time limit for that choice, or no confirmation (26(2)); the choice is confirmed on a durable medium (26(3)); where confirmation is chosen, at least the information of Article 6(1), points (a) to (e), (h) to (k), (o) and (p), of Directive 2011/83/EU (26(4)(a)); disclosure of any payment the trader receives for proposing a contract and of any conflict of interest, after which the consumer must confirm that contract whatever the earlier choice (26(4)(b)); the trader and the provider of the system may identify and authenticate themselves with a European Business Wallet or a European Digital Identity Wallet (26(5)), and European Business Wallets may also identify the system and establish on whose behalf it acts (26(6)); the consumer's system transmits the contact details needed for performance (26(7)); the trader confirms the contract on a durable medium (26(8)); traders must not design interfaces that require consumers to use automated systems (26(9)); Article 26 does not apply to the provision of financial services (26(10)). Article 27: where both sides contract solely through automated systems, the trader may give the Article 6(1) information only in a commonly used machine-readable format, is exempt from Article 6a, and Articles 8(1) to (4) and (8) of Directive 2011/83/EU do not apply, though a durable-medium confirmation is still due. Article 40: in force on the twentieth day after publication in the Official Journal; applies from [12 months after the entry into force], bracketed in the proposal. Recitals 77 to 81 explain these rules. A proposal, not law; it names no agent protocol.

title: The "Payment" HTTP Authentication Scheme (draft-httpauth-payment-01, repository text of 2026-11-11)
publisher: Tempo Labs and Stripe (B. Ryan, J. Moxey, T. Meagher, J. Weinstein, S. Kaliski)
notes: Read in research/vendor/mpp-specs with git show origin/main at merge commit 7bb99c8542252b7aa4230c184e48f16c0ea1427a (PR #404, merged 2026-11-11T18:24:35Z). Edited in place under the -01 name, with no revision bump and no Datatracker submission. The rewritten section on other authentication schemes calls a Bearer token, HTTP Message Signatures (RFC 9421) or an attestation in an application-defined header field 'other authentication', which the Payment scheme does not define, register or constrain. Servers SHOULD verify it first and answer 401 (or the mechanism's own error) or 403 before any 402; when a request carries a Payment credential, servers MUST verify the other authentication before verifying, consuming or settling the credential, and on a denial on that basis MUST NOT settle, consume the challenge or credential, or issue a Payment-Receipt. The header parameter moves from MAY to SHOULD when the other authentication uses Authorization. Clients MUST resend their other authentication on the paid retry and MAY resend the same credential after a 401, or after a 403 whose Problem Details say other authentication denied access and nothing settled. Other mechanisms MAY bind their proofs to the challenge id; the draft defines no such binding. 403 now has two meanings, and servers SHOULD say which in the Problem Details body. A new security section scopes other authentication credentials to their origin and forbids sending them on a cross-origin redirect. The status codes table and the fields in the site's field tables are otherwise unchanged since 50309c8, apart from example fixes of 2026-10-26. At the same commit specs/intents still holds only the charge and subscription intents and specs/methods the same 11 method folders, and a git grep of specs/ finds none of the SDK header names Identity-Attestation, Identity-Attestation-Required, Identity-Presentation or Identity-Required.

notes: Read through the .md twin on 2026-11-14 (HTTP 200). MCP 2026-07-28 makes the protocol stateless: it removes the initialize and notifications/initialized handshake, so each request carries its protocol version and client capabilities in _meta, and servers MUST implement server/discover to advertise versions and capabilities; it also removes protocol sessions and the Mcp-Session-Id header (SEP-2567, SEP-2575). MCP's versioning page, read the same day, names 2026-07-28 the current protocol version. The same URL is recorded as src-orbit-mcp-changelog-2026-07-28 in research/orbit.c.sources.json.

title: MCP specification 2026-07-28, Basic: Error Codes
notes: Read 2026-11-21 from docs/specification/2026-07-28/basic/index.mdx on the main branch of modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol (gh api raw). The Error Codes section is identical to commit db4bfcf (2026-07-28), although the file had other edits on 2026-11-16 and 2026-11-18. It treats -32000 to -32019 as legacy and reserves -32020 to -32099 for codes the MCP specification defines, which implementations must not emit unless defined; it defines -32020 to -32022 and lists -32002 and -32042 (URL elicitation required, 2025-11-25 only) as earlier codes that implementations of this version must not emit; new application codes should sit outside -32768 to -32000.

title: wevm/mppx commit b2b1a0b: fix for CVE-2026-34210 in the stripe/charge server
notes: Merge commit of 2026-03-26 that fixed GHSA-8mhj-rffc-rcvw (CVE-2026-34210) in src/stripe/server/Charge.ts: it reads Stripe's Idempotent-Replayed response header and rejects a replayed PaymentIntent with a verification-failed error. In the parent code, the same as tag mppx@0.4.10, both PaymentIntent paths already set the idempotency key to mppx_ followed by the challenge id and the SPT, so a replayed credential got Stripe's cached PaymentIntent back. title: mppx PR #1184: fix: enforce payment boundaries across HTTP and subscription flows
notes: gh api 2026-11-21: opened 2026-11-06T17:07:41Z, merged 2026-11-18T16:59:23Z, released in mppx 0.21.0 (2026-11-19) as the minor, breaking change 7b47ff2. It closes five payment-boundary gaps: the Express adapter holds JSON, raw and streamed output until payment verification succeeds; disconnects and streaming errors are handled; custom subscription clients must declare a chain that matches the challenge; proxy replay keys are bound to an explicitly configured payment authority and the route scope (enabling replay without a stable authority fails at startup); the CLI refuses to sign after non-loopback cleartext hops or with TLS verification off, and x402 credential destinations are limited to the challenge origin. No GHSA or CVE.

title: mppx PR #1300: fix: require prepaid work and payer binding for sessions
notes: gh api 2026-11-21: opened 2026-11-16T13:56:56Z, merged 2026-11-16T15:19:37Z, released in mppx 0.20.0 (2026-11-16) as the minor, breaking change e2d81d0, which also added MIGRATING.md. Motivation: session retries could bypass stream metering, automatic generators could start work before charging, and opens could attribute payment to a different source account. Summary: re-run payment verification for session proxy retries, require manual charges for billable per-item streams, bind opening credential sources to the transaction payer. No GHSA or CVE.

title: mppx PR #1304: feat(identity): add ERC-8004 agent identity provider
notes: gh api 2026-11-21: opened 2026-11-16T15:48:31Z by brendanjryan, merged 2026-11-16T16:12:02Z (squash commit d8292be), released in mppx 0.20.0 (npm 2026-11-16T16:23:31Z, the first version that exports ./extensions/identity/erc8004; the CHANGELOG lists it under patch changes). Code read with git show 6056a5b in research/vendor/mppx (the folder is unchanged since d8292be). Constants.ts: type erc8004 (advertised in Identity-Required), chainId 4217 (Tempo mainnet), identityRegistry 0x8004A169FB4a3325136EB29fA0ceB6D2e539a432, rpcUrl https://rpc.tempo.xyz, headers Agent-Id (eip155:<chainId>:<registry>:<agentId>) and Agent-Signature (<created>.<nonce>.<signature>), maxAge 300 and clockTolerance 60 seconds. The client prover signs an EIP-191 message over mppx:erc8004, the agent ID, the method and URL, a created time and a nonce. The server calls only getAgentWallet on the registry and isValidSignature (ERC-1271) on the wallet; a zero wallet is forbidden; agents of another registry or chain are rejected; a signature is single-use only with a store, otherwise replayable for six minutes. paymentCheck accepts a tempo charge transaction or proof credential whose did:pkh source is the agent's wallet and otherwise requires the request signature (no credential, hash credentials, sessions, Zones, other methods); the PR body's line that it refuses Zone payments describes an earlier iteration. An optional allow(agent) hook receives id, agentId and wallet. The proxy and cross-origin redirects drop both headers.

title: mppx PR #1307: feat(tempo): accept TIP-1166 configurable account vouchers in sessions
notes: gh api 2026-11-21: opened 2026-11-16T16:41:24Z, merged 2026-11-20T11:03:29Z. Servers accept configurable-account (0x05) vouchers and close authorizations when configurableVouchers is set (default false) and advertise it in the challenge; configurable-account clients refuse to open against servers that do not advertise it.

title: mppx PR #1315: fix: only accept Payment-Authorization as a challenge credential header
notes: gh api 2026-11-21: opened 2026-11-16T20:52:46Z, merged 2026-11-17T16:38:48Z, released in mppx 0.21.0 (2026-11-19, changeset 58513ac); closes issue #1306. Before it, an explicit header of Authorization or an empty value was normalized away, and any other token, such as X-Payment, was accepted and paid; git show 9405660:src/Challenge.ts in research/vendor/mppx shows credentialHeader() returning the challenge's header value or Authorization, so the client sent the credential in the named field. Now clients skip a challenge that names another header, a credential echoes the server's spelling of Payment-Authorization, and a server configured with a header other than Authorization or Payment-Authorization throws when it builds the challenge. pympp 0.26.0 made the same change (#437). No GHSA or CVE.

title: mppx PR #1325: fix: preserve replay claims owned by newer requests
notes: gh api 2026-11-21: opened 2026-11-18T14:41:39Z, merged 2026-11-18T18:28:11Z, released in mppx 0.21.0 (2026-11-19, changeset 7300c80). Motivation: a failed payment request could remove a newer request's replay claim after its own claim expired, so the same payment could authorize another response. Fix: replay claims are bound to a unique request owner and deleted atomically only by it. No GHSA or CVE.

title: mppx PR #1326: fix: bind session credential identity to the funding payer
notes: gh api 2026-11-21: opened 2026-11-18T14:44:57Z, merged 2026-11-18T16:39:24Z, released in mppx 0.21.0 (2026-11-19, changeset b457436). Motivation: a delegated signer could identify itself as the paying account while spending another account's session channel, so policy applied to the funding account was bypassed. Fix: existing session credentials must name the channel payer, while delegated voucher signatures stay valid. No GHSA or CVE.

title: mppx PR #1332: fix: bind ERC-8004 verification to a trusted origin
notes: gh api 2026-11-21: opened 2026-11-19T16:09:05Z by brendanjryan, open and not merged. The motivation says a relayed ERC-8004 signature can authenticate at another service when the request URL is derived from an attacker-controlled Host; the change adds an optional origin setting and says deployments must configure it or enforce trusted hosts at ingress. The author's statement, not an advisory.

title: MPP session method drafts (tempo, evm, hedera, solana, xrpl, lightning) at commit 50309c8
notes: Read 2026-10-21 in the clone at commit 50309c8. Expiry rules by session draft: tempo, evm and hedera channels have no expiry and their vouchers no validity field, and each draft says servers should settle and close channels inactive for about 30 days or more. solana: the server closes a channel after a negotiated idle timeout of 1 second to 30 days, and a voucher can carry an optional expiresAt. xrpl: ledger channels can carry Expiration or CancelAfter, the server must refuse vouchers within a margin of either, and after CancelAfter anyone may delete the channel and the deposit returns to the funder. lightning: sessions have no built-in expiry, and servers should enforce an idle timeout, 5 minutes recommended.

Integration row 'Payment channels and MPP sessions': deposits made before the upgrade still settle but cannot be topped up, so close channels first if they need more funds; a configurable account cannot sign its own vouchers under T14 and needs a separate single-key authorizedSigner until TIP-1166 in T15.

Verify requires a payment to the deposit address in USDC on Base, a Tempo payout address in paymentRequirements.extra.tempoSettlement, address screening and room in the Tempo payout buffer. Settle says the Tempo amount equals the Base amount, with no fee by default and network fees paid by Tempo's treasury, but the payout object keeps a required fee field described as a flat fee withheld, and the guide gives no fee. Tempo's pages therefore do not settle fees or payout timing, and the atlas states neither.

title: Tempo x402 facilitator (Tempo docs guide)
notes: Read 2026-11-21 through its Markdown twin (HTTP 200); the page carries no date. Sellers keep selling over x402 and point their middleware at https://api.tempo.xyz/v1/x402: buyers pay USDC on Base mainnet (eip155:8453) with the exact scheme (EIP-3009 or Permit2), and each payment arrives as OUSD on Tempo mainnet (eip155:4217) at the payout address named in extra.tempoSettlement. An API key with the mpp:write scope and that payout address are all a seller needs; no minimum, and a per-payment maximum that Tempo sets. Testnet facilitator: https://api.tempo-dev.workers.dev/v1/x402 (Base Sepolia USDC in, Moderato OUSD out). The guide says the OUSD arrives a few minutes after Base is final, while the API reference (src-stripe-mpp-tempo-x402-api) says settle broadcasts the payout without waiting for a receipt, so the atlas states no payout timing. Dating: tempoxyz/mpp PR #1255 added the facilitator section to mpp.dev on 2026-11-18 while asking to wait for production (src-stripe-mpp-gh-mpp-pr-1255); mppx 0.21.1 (2026-11-19) exports tempoX402(), and the public /supported route answered on 2026-11-21 (src-stripe-mpp-tempo-x402-supported). title: Frequently Asked Questions, Google UCP Guide
notes: Read 2026-10-20 (page last updated 2026-10-16) and again 2026-11-14 through the .md twin (last updated 2026-11-03 UTC; the 2026-10-30 version differed only by an MCP question). Still says: merchant is MoR, PSP must process Google tokens, PAN_ONLY, Google-UCP-Prober/1.0 health checks, order data retained until the user requests deletion. Changed between 2026-10-20 and 2026-10-30: checkout requests carry UCP-Agent and a User-Agent of Google-Shopping-Merchant-Integration, Google/UCP* or Google-UCP-Prober/1.0; discovery and OAuth client_credentials requests carry no UCP-Agent; Account Linking uses OpenAuth or Google-AccountLinking-Fetcher/1.0; headers alone must not authenticate. Verification methods are now mutual TLS against Google's UCP Root CAs, ES256 RFC 9421 signatures checked against the keys at https://ucp.goog/.well-known/ucp.json (24-hour cache, refetch on an unknown kid) and source-ASN rules (AS15169; AS396982 for Account Linking). The earlier wording (the User-Agent begins with Google/UCP; verify by reverse DNS or published IP range files) has been replaced. Read again through the .md twin on 2026-11-21 (still last updated 2026-11-03): unchanged on the points above; at launch a UCP integration powers AI Mode in Google Search and the Gemini web and mobile apps; AP2 can be used as a specialized payment layer within UCP; no fee text.

title: Grocery ordering (Google UCP Guide, UCP in connected apps)
notes: Read through the .md twin on 2026-11-21 (HTTP 200); footer 'Last updated 2026-11-17 UTC'; Google's Latest updates page lists it under October 2026 as the grocery ordering guide for version 2026-08-25. It describes a sample integration between the Google Agent and a retailer: search_locations, search_catalog, create_cart, update_cart, get_cart, lookup_locations (called whenever the cart UI is rendered) and cancel_cart. create_cart, update_cart and get_cart return a continue_url to the retailer's checkout for the final delivery address, time window and payment; cancel_cart returns the cart state before deletion. MCP and REST are both supported, with MCP recommended for Connected Apps. The flow assumes the Google Account is already linked to the retailer account (OAuth 2.1). Required scopes: dev.ucp.common.location.search:read, dev.ucp.common.location.lookup:read, dev.ucp.shopping.catalog.search:read, dev.ucp.shopping.catalog.lookup:read and dev.ucp.shopping.cart:manage; dev.ucp.shopping.checkout:manage and dev.ucp.shopping.order:manage are optional, for integrations that also support UCP checkout or order management. buyer_address_locations and context.buyer_address_location are Google-specific vendor extensions. The guide calls Request-Id an optional request identifier, while the UCP REST OpenAPI marks it required at v2026-08-25 and on main.

notes: Read through the .md twin on 2026-11-14 (2026-11-15T03:01Z UTC). title: Visa Core Rules and Visa Product and Service Rules (2026-10-24 edition)
notes: Text of the 2026-10-24 edition read 2026-11-14 (PDF Last-Modified 2026-10-29, 936 pages); the 2026-04-18 edition was read on 2026-10-18 and rechecked on 2026-10-19. The October edition renumbers the agent section from 4.1.24 (pages 254 to 260 in April) to 4.1.23, Agentic Platform Requirements (pages 263 to 269), with the same rule IDs (ID# 0031167 to 0031177, each marked Last Updated Apr 2026); its summary of changes since the April edition lists no agentic change. One public document holds both rulebooks; the agent rules sit mainly in the Visa Product and Service Rules. 1.1.1.5 (ID# 0007428): the rules govern the relationship between Visa and its Members and their agents and confer no rights on third parties. 1.1.1.3 (ID# 0000385): where the rules conflict with applicable laws or regulations, the laws govern. 4.1.23.2 (ID# 0031168; 4.1.24.2 in April): an Agentic Payment Provider must enroll in and comply with the Visa Intelligent Commerce program and register with Visa, directly or via an Agentic Payment Enabler; obtain a Token from Visa or an Agentic Payment Enabler when it uses a Stored Credential; and not undertake an Agentic Transaction in a Card-Present Environment or aggregate several Agentic Transactions into one. 4.1.23.10 (ID# 0031176; 4.1.24.10 in April): a Cardholder is responsible for any actions an Agentic Payment Provider takes as part of an Agentic Transaction as if the Cardholder initiated the Transaction. Glossary, Cardholder (ID# 0024372): an Agentic Payment Provider is considered the Cardholder for an Agentic Transaction. Glossary, Agentic Payment Provider (ID# 0031164): the provider of an application a Cardholder uses for tasks on the Cardholder's behalf, which can search, discover and purchase on a payment instruction and Cardholder verification, can undertake an Agentic Transaction, can be used at more than one Merchant, stores and transmits a Token (an EMV payment token, ID# 0029108), completes a Transaction by passing the Token to the Merchant, and takes no part in authorization, clearing or settlement. 1.7.6.1 (ID# 0006558): an Issuer must pay the Acquirer for an Agentic Transaction processed in accordance with a Cardholder's payment instructions. 1.7.4.1 (ID# 0029326): an Issuer must not block or decline transactions, including those of Agentic Payment Providers, in a systematic or wholesale manner, with listed exceptions (an immediate fraud threat, law, the rules; a footnote excludes Chile). 5.4.2.5 (ID# 0008771): a Merchant must not require a Cardholder to waive the right to dispute a Transaction, including an Agentic Transaction. 1.5.5.2 (ID# 0006948): a Merchant, Agentic Payment Enabler or Agentic Payment Provider must not surcharge, with regional exceptions. Dispute Condition 10.4, invalid disputes (ID# 0030254): for disputes processed on or after 2026-10-24, the matching data from earlier undisputed transactions includes login IDs for an Agentic Payment Provider. The archived copy (captured 2025-11-24) is the 2025-10-18 edition, which lists these rules under 'Global Agentic Payments/Visa Intelligent Commerce (VIC) Program Launched', effective 2025-10-18 (2025-11-04 in Chile). Every mention of 'Agentic' in the April 2026 edition was read: Visa calls none of these rules a liability shift, none adds an agent-specific dispute condition, interchange rate or fee, and the text does not mention TAP, 8004, ERC-, x402, ACP, UCP or AP2. In the October 2026 edition 'Trusted Agent' has no hits, 'liability shift' appears only in EMV contexts, and the dispute-evidence rule (Dispute Condition 10.4, in force for disputes processed from 2026-10-24) is unchanged in substance. Visa omits proprietary and security details from the public edition. Rechecked 2026-11-21: the PDF now answers with Last-Modified 2026-11-20, but its XMP creation and modification dates (2026-10-23) and its 936 pages match the 2026-10-24 edition, so the edition is unchanged. A text check the same day found the Summary of Changes still headed as changes since the 18 April 2026 rules, the agent section still 4.1.23 Agentic Platform Requirements, and still no hits for 'Trusted Agent'; the rules were not re-read in full.

notes: Read with git show at origin/main d062df6 (2026-11-14) in research/vendor/mpp; the file last changed in 91a3996 (2026-11-12). title: Visa Intelligent Commerce developer documentation (overview, concepts, workflows and production readiness pages)
notes: Replaced the public VIC overview in October 2026. On 2026-10-19 the rendered overview asked visitors to sign in, and its text and the concepts (/docs/visa-intelligent-commerce/concepts) and workflows (/docs/visa-intelligent-commerce/workflows) pages were read from the page source. On 2026-11-14 the overview, concepts, workflows and production-readiness pages and their .md twins answered HTTP 200 with no sign-in prompt. The overview then said production access requires onboarding to VIC and to the Trusted Agent Protocol, Visa Token Service and Visa Payment Passkeys, plus registration through the Visa Agent Registry Service (VARS) so that Visa can validate agent signatures and merchant encryption keys at credential retrieval. The concepts page said agentSignature is required when the agent is a Trusted Agent Provider or the token requestor is a Wallet Provider and is not sent for an Open Source Agent; instructions default to a 30-day intent expiration in the US; at most 15 cryptograms per token in a rolling 24 hours; the restricted MCC list sits in a VIC and TAP Client Implementation Guide, named without a link; and US merchants that support 3-D Secure receive a Program Not Supported response for agentic transactions in the US only, while other regions keep 3DS with region-specific treatment and SCA in Europe uses Visa Payment Passkeys. The production-readiness page said Visa's CE3.0 program covers agentic transactions. Card enrollment journey (read 2026-10-19): token provisioned through VTS first, then issuer step-up where required and, if applicable, Visa Payment Passkey setup with device binding; credential retrieval only after that unless the use case is approved to skip the passkey. Workflows (read 2026-10-19; the authentication step reads the same on 2026-11-14): the consumer authenticates the instruction through a Visa Payment Passkey or other issuer-approved methods; the agent submits the credential to the merchant checkout or a PSP-enabled flow; Visa retains post-purchase confirmation data for disputes. No fees or pricing were stated on either date. Rechecked 2026-11-21 (HTTP 200): the overview still gives the production onboarding requirements (TAP, VTS, VPP, VARS registration) and states no fees; the concepts .md twin still gives the US 3-D Secure behavior.

title: Visa Merchant Registry Service (VMRS) in the Trusted Agent Protocol API reference
notes: Read 2026-11-14 (HTTP 200) from this .md twin and from the OpenAPI 3.1.0 document embedded in https://developer.visa.com/api-reference/trusted-agent-protocol/get-v1-trustedagentprotocol (info.title Trusted Agent Protocol, version 1, server https://sandbox.api.visa.com). Tag Visa Merchant Registry Service, described as a micro service that manages merchant identities and distributes encryption keys for payment request encryption in the TAP ecosystem; navigation bundle TRAP.102, public. Nine operations: POST /vmrs/v1/merchants (201; 409 when the merchantUrl already exists; 422); GET and PUT /vmrs/v1/merchants/{merchantId}; GET and POST /vmrs/v1/merchants/{merchantId}/keys (new keys are created deactivated); GET, PUT and DELETE /vmrs/v1/merchants/{merchantId}/keys/{keyId}; POST /vmrs/v1/merchants/{merchantId}/keys/{keyId}/activate. 15 schemas. MerchantCreate requires indicator (TAP, ACG or BOTH; described only as the transaction processing type), merchantName and merchantUrl; optional vmid, encryptionKey (KeyCreate), cryptogramType (TAVV or DAVV, default DAVV), apiIntegrations and webIntegrations (url, integrationSpec, metadata), paymentPayloadType (UNENCRYPTED or ENCRYPTED, default UNENCRYPTED), protocolInteractions (protocol ucp, acp or x402, with url, documentationUrl and metadata) and acceptanceRelationships (example visa, mastercard). KeyCreate requires keyName, algorithm (RSA-OAEP, RSA-OAEP-256, RSA-OAEP-384 or RSA-OAEP-512, a key wrapping algorithm), encryptionKey (a Base64-encoded asymmetric public key in DER, PEM, JWK or OpenSSH format) and encryptionType (A256GCM, A128GCM, C20P, A256CBC_HS512, A128CBC_HS256, A256CCM or A128CCM, a content encryption algorithm); expirationDate is optional and must be in the future. A CredentialsResponse schema (vmid, merchantId, merchantName, merchantUrl, encryptionKey, cryptogramType, paymentPayloadType) is referenced by no path. No security scheme is declared. Not in the reference on 2026-10-19 (see src-visa-tap-apiref).

Preview of AgentCore payments, built with Coinbase and Stripe: a Coinbase CDP or Stripe Privy wallet as the payment connection, session-level spending limits enforced by AgentCore, x402 negotiation when an agent meets an HTTP 402, and the Coinbase x402 Bazaar MCP server (over 10,000 x402 endpoints) through AgentCore Gateway. Preview Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt) and Asia Pacific (Sydney). The AWS Machine Learning Blog post of the same day says that at preview it supports the x402 protocol, with more protocols on the roadmap.

title: Process a payment (Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide)
notes: Read the .md twin on 2026-11-21. Payment types CRYPTO_X402, MPP and AWS_BILLING_X402. AWS Billing: pass the accepts entry whose network is aws:base unchanged, with the seller-signed quote token in extra.quoteToken and the service-managed instrument aws.agentcorepayments.awsbilling.v1; optional options.dpopJwk binds the token per RFC 9449 (P-256, P-384 or P-521); paymentToken is a signed JWT valid for 5 minutes, sent within 5 minutes as an x402 version 2 PAYMENT-SIGNATURE with payload {paymentToken}; a single AWS Billing payment must be greater than USD $0.00 and cannot exceed USD $10,000.00. MPP: forward exactly one WWW-Authenticate: Payment header in paymentInput.mpp; AgentCore checks the budget, signs and returns a ready-to-send Authorization value; charge intent only, with methods evm (canonical USDC), tempo and solana (server-sponsored fees only); Coinbase CDP and Stripe (Privy) connectors, solana with Stripe (Privy) only; buyerPaysGasFees gives fee consent.

title: Listing Agentic Commerce products (AWS Marketplace Seller Guide)
notes: Read the .md twin on 2026-11-21. Agentic Commerce supports only the x402 protocol; it is available in US East (N. Virginia) (us-east-1) and quotes are in USD; the seller registers a quote-signing key as a JWKS URL or an AWS KMS key; the product ID is the route's payTo and the quote's settlement.product_id claim; Marketplace rejects quotes without that claim or without aud aws:marketplace, scheme exact and network aws:base, with a price above 100,000 or more than 8 decimal places, or valid for more than 30 days; the reserved dimension agentic_commerce_default meters one unit per US dollar; refunds are standard billing adjustments applied to an invoice, with no API for individual payments.

title: AWS Marketplace now supports agentic payments with AgentCore
notes: postDateTime 2026-11-19T21:30:00Z, read 2026-11-21. AI agents buy select AWS Marketplace products and pay per request in US dollars over x402 through AgentCore payments; charges settle on the customer's existing AWS bill with no crypto wallet; customers can set spending limits, approved sellers and guardrails, Private Marketplace policies still apply, and transactions appear in AWS CloudTrail and AWS Cost Explorer; sellers integrate the AWS Marketplace x402 SDK and are paid through Marketplace seller disbursements. The post says the capability is available in all Regions where AgentCore payments is available and does not label it preview or generally available.

title: How AI traffic monetization works (AWS WAF Developer Guide)
notes: Read the .md twin on 2026-11-21: the 402 lists a USDC price, Base and Solana, payTo, a maximum timeout and the scheme; verification is synchronous at the edge; after a 2xx origin fetch the payment is settled on chain through Coinbase Developer Platform's x402 facilitator before the content is served; settlement is skipped and the client not charged when the origin returns 4xx or 5xx. The page names only x402.

title: AWS WAF announces AI traffic monetization
notes: postDateTime 2026-06-15T12:00:00Z, read 2026-11-21. A new AWS WAF Bot Control capability returns HTTP 402 using x402 with prices, accepted payment methods and license terms; WAF verifies the proof of payment at the edge, issues a scoped access token and serves the response in one request cycle; policies can depend on verification status, Web Bot Auth signatures included; settlement and verification are provided by Coinbase's x402 Facilitator; Stripe direct account payments and Machine Payments Protocol (MPP) support are coming soon; no additional charge beyond standard AWS WAF charges; available where WAF web ACLs are associated with Amazon CloudFront distributions.

title: Scheme: batch-settlement on SVM (at commit e35bf88)
notes: Compared with 1a08434 through the GitHub compare API on 2026-11-21 (PR #4222). A concurrent duplicate /settle for one transaction must be rejected with duplicate_settlement, not coalesced into a shared success (the old text allowed either for client-supplied deposit and refund transactions); a retry is valid only for settlement_pending; close retries fail with invalid_batch_settlement_svm_close_state and claims at or below the settled watermark with invalid_batch_settlement_svm_cumulative_amount_mismatch; settle responses may carry extra.channelStates[] (channelId, status, balance, totalClaimed, payoutWatermark, withdrawRequestedAt), which a server adopts only after stated checks; a server must not fall back to an implicit public RPC endpoint. The EVM and SVM batch-settlement files were the only files under specs/ that changed from 1a08434 to e35bf88.
